LLM · 03 · The harness

From a model to a system: the harness around GPT

The previous deck ended with a trained GPT: a function from token ids to next-token logits, and a loop that samples from it. That function has no memory, no sense of when to stop, no hands and no eyes. This deck is the journey from that function to a system that answers, remembers, acts, refuses, and can be measured: the harness. Every number comes from running your own model inside a sixty-line harness written for this deck.

  • Press Enter to reveal the next piece of a slide; the dots at the bottom centre count the steps. The notes panel (N) gives every slide from three angles: Visually (what the picture is), Mathematically (the rule or the cost), Numerically (the real numbers, measured by running your model), then where it lives in your code and a question to check yourself.
  • The model is the tiny GPT of deck 02, retrained in a fresh process for this deck: CharTokenizer on the -character corpus , GPT(18, 16, 2, 2, max_seq_len=16), parameters, Adam steps, loss in s. The four scratch-only workarounds from the deck 02 recap were applied; nothing in src/ was changed.
  • The harness itself (Engine, KVCache, Context, tools, policy, loop, trace, evals) is a scratch script of about sixty lines of plain NumPy and Python around your modules. Slides show its code; every trace, timing and score on the slides is its real output.

The story in one paragraph

GPT.forward maps ids to logits and keeps no state between calls. To make it useful, something outside the model must choose a token from each logits row and decide when to stop (the engine), decide what the slots of the window contain (context management), run the model again after a tool was used (the agent loop), execute what the model asked for only if a rule allows it (tools and the policy gate), record what happened (observability), score it against fixed inputs (evaluation) and expose it to many users (serving). All of that is ordinary, deterministic, testable code; the model is the only stochastic part, and it is the only part that is not code. That split, stateless core inside stateful machinery, is what the word harness means, whether the core is a model, a function under test, or a benchmark subject.

01 · Recap · What the model is

Recap: GPT is a pure function from ids to logits

Two calls with the same ids give the same logits. Nothing is kept between calls: no memory of a conversation, a user, a tool, or a reason to stop. Everything that makes the function usable lives outside it.

forward:

Embedding, blocks under a causal mask, final LayerNorm, head. Row of the output scores every vocabulary entry as the token after position . The weights are the only thing the function "knows".

generate: the one loop the model ships with

Forward, take the last row, divide by , softmax, sample, append, repeat max_new_tokens times. No stop rule, no window crop, no cache, no record of what happened: a loop, not a harness.

02 · The challenge

The challenge: a function is not a product

Ask the trained model to write from "the " and six things go wrong that no training can repair, because each is a decision made outside the forward pass. Each gap names a part of the harness.

What happens today

GPT.generate(Tensor([[16, 9, 7, 1]]), 20) runs forwards and then raises Sequence length exceeds maximum: 17 > 16. With a crop added, it writes characters of corpus phrases and only stops because the count ran out.

Six decisions the model cannot make

When to stop. What the window contains. Whether to run again after a tool. Whether an action is allowed. How to answer fast. What happened and how well. None is a logits question; each is a line of code around the model.

Definition

The harness is everything that drives a model, feeds it, acts on its output, limits it and measures it. The model stays a pure function; the harness holds all state and all rules.

Error text captured from GPT.generate on the trained model; the -character run is Engine.stream(prompt "the ", , seed 1, cropped) from the scratch harness: "dog ate the bun . the cat ate the rat . the dog ate the bun ".

Visually

  • Step 1: a user, the model box, and the raw output: a stream that never ends by itself and a crash at token .
  • Steps 2–7: the six gaps appear one by one around the model, each with the colour of the harness part that will close it: engine (stop, speed), context (memory), loop (act again), policy (allow), observability and evaluation (watch, score). The colours are kept for the rest of the deck.

Mathematically

The model is a conditional distribution . A product needs a decision procedure: a function from (user input, history, tool results, rules) to (what to show, what to run, when to stop). Only one factor of that procedure, the next-token distribution, is learned. The rest is a program, and because it is a program it can be tested, logged and changed without retraining.

Numerically

In your code

Nothing in src/ implements any of the six decisions yet; the roadmap's tiny-LM milestone asks only for "generate tokens autoregressively". The scratch harness of this deck adds them outside the package; the recap slide lists which ones are worth moving into src/.

Check yourself

  • Could a bigger model learn to stop by itself? It can learn to emit an end token with high probability, but something outside must still read that token and break the loop: the decision stays in the harness.

02 · What a harness is

Three harnesses, one shape: drive, observe, judge

A test harness drives a function with fixed inputs and checks the outputs. An eval harness drives a model with a benchmark and scores it. An agent harness drives a model with a goal and acts on the output.

Test harness

Core: a function. Drive: fixed inputs. Observe: return values and exceptions. Judge: assertions. Your src/tests is one.

Evaluation harness

Core: a model. Drive: a benchmark of prompts. Observe: generations or log-probabilities. Judge: a scorer. Section 06 builds one for the tiny model.

Agent harness

Core: a model. Drive: a user's goal plus tool results. Observe: the text it emits. Judge: a parser and a policy, then act and loop. This is the one this deck builds.

The design rule they share

The core is replaceable and holds no state. The harness holds all state, all rules and all measurement, and it is plain code.

The Trainer in src/core/training.py is a fourth: it drives the model with batches, observes the loss, judges with the optimizer. Slide 20 compares it with the agent loop line by line.

Visually

  • Steps 1–3: three rings with the same three arrows (drive, observe, judge) around a different core. Step 4: the three collapse onto one template with the core left blank.

Mathematically

A harness is a function . Fixing the core and the rules gives a map from inputs to outputs that can be tested like any other; changing the core (a new checkpoint, a new model) keeps unchanged. That separation is what makes "swap the model" a one-line change.

Numerically

In the scratch harness the core is one function: cached_step(model, cache, ids) → logits row. The agent loop, the evaluation and the streaming demo all call only it. Replacing the tiny GPT with the random , model used for the cache timings needed no other change.

In your code

Trainer.train_epoch is the same shape: drive (dataloader), observe (loss), judge (optimizer.step), with state in self.history, self.step, self.epoch. The model passed in is any object with forward and parameters().

Check yourself

  • Which of the three harnesses needs the model to be stochastic? None: sampling is the engine's choice; with all three are deterministic.

02 · What a harness is · Anatomy

Anatomy: seven parts around one stateless model

Read from the inside out: each layer uses only the layer inside it and owns one kind of state. Sections 03 to 06 walk through the layers in this order.

Inside: the model and the engine

The engine turns logits into tokens: sampling policy, stop rules, budget, KV cache, streaming. Its state is the cache and the token count.

Middle: context and the loop

Context decides what the slots hold. The loop renders the context, calls the engine, parses, and decides to answer, call a tool or stop. Its state is the message list and the step count.

Outside: policy, observability, serving

The policy gate sits between parse and execute. Observability records every event; evaluation replays fixed inputs through the same loop; serving runs many loops for many users.

Two rules

State flows outward only: the model holds none, the engine a cache, the loop the history, the server the sessions. Decisions are code; only the next token is learned.

Layer names are the class and function names of the scratch harness: cached_step / KVCache, Engine.stream, Context, agent_loop with TOOLS and POLICY, trace, the eval block. The same split appears in production harnesses under other names.

Visually

  • Steps 1–7: rings grow outward from the model: engine, context, loop, tools and policy, observability, evaluation, serving. The colour of each ring is used for that component on every later slide. The small labels name the state each ring owns.

Mathematically

Layering as function composition: . Each layer is a function of the layer inside plus its own state ; the model is the base case with . A request's full behaviour is determined by , which is why recording and the seed (observability) makes any run reproducible.

Numerically

State sizes for the tiny model: cache floats; the loop's context after the tool demo: messages, characters; a trace of events. For GPT-2 small the cache alone is floats MiB per sequence in float32.

In your code

Nothing of this exists in src/ beyond generate; in the scratch script each ring is – lines. The order of the sections that follow is the order of the rings.

Check yourself

  • Why must the policy gate be outside the loop's parser rather than a tool itself? A tool is something the model chooses; the gate must apply to every choice, so it is code the model cannot bypass.

03 · Engine · Decoding

Decoding: one logits row becomes one token, by policy

The model hands over scores. The engine decides how they become a choice: argmax, sample as is, sharpen or flatten with , or cut the tail first. Same weights, different behaviour: the policy is a harness setting.

03 · Engine · Stop rules and budgets

Stop rules and budgets: when the engine goes quiet

A model never stops; it always has a next token. The engine ends the loop for one of three reasons: a stop token or string appeared, the budget ran out, or the window is full. The reason is part of the output.

GPT.generate: no crop, so the window overflows

Prompt ids + 13th new token max_seq_len : ValueError from PositionalEncoding. The fix is one slice, tokens[:, −T:], before every forward.

Budget: max_new_tokens

tokens requested, produced, reason budget. Without a stop rule the model recites the corpus until the count runs out.

Stop strings and stop tokens

With stop string " . " the same run ends after tokens: "dog ate the bun . ", reason stop. Chat models use a dedicated end token (<|end|>, section 04) and the harness checks for it after every token.

The engine returns the reason

stop, budget, or window: the loop uses it. A budget ending inside a tool call means "ask for more or give up", a stop means "parse this".

Three runs from "the ", : GPT.generate(…, max_new_tokens=20) as shipped (error text captured; its first twelve characters are drawn from the seed-1 run, the shipped loop uses the module rng), Engine.stream(max_new=60, seed 1) and the same with stop_strs=(" . ",). Characters are the real outputs.

Visually

  • Step 1: the shipped loop: twelve characters, then a red cross at the 13th forward, where would be .
  • Step 2: the budgeted run: sixty character chips, cropped to the window every step, ending only because the count reached .
  • Step 3: the same seed with a stop string: identical first characters (same rng, same model), then the loop breaks at " . ".
  • Step 4: the three reasons as the engine's return value.

Mathematically

Generation is a loop with an exit predicate: stop if text ends with any stop_strs, or max_new, or (without a cache rebuild) len(ids) . Checking the predicate after every token is what makes a stop rule exact: the token that completes the stop string is the last one produced. With a single end token id , the predicate is , which is cheaper and unambiguous.

Numerically

Free run: , ms per token, ends budget. Stop run: , ends stop. Greedy from "the ": the same characters as the seed-1 sample: the sampler happened to pick the argmax 'd' () at the first step and never left the argmax afterwards. breaks the recitation once ("rgat") in tokens.

In your code

GPT.generate loops for _ in range(max_new_tokens) with no other exit and no crop. The scratch Engine.stream crops the prompt to the last ids, checks text.endswith(s) after each token, yields (token, ms, reason) and returns after a stop. It is a generator, so the caller sees tokens as they are produced.

Check yourself

  • Why check the stop string on the decoded text rather than on ids? A stop string may span several tokens with a BPE tokenizer; the text is the only reliable place to see it.

03 · Engine · The KV cache

The KV cache: never recompute what the past told you

Writing token needs and of all earlier positions. generate recomputes them every step; a cache stores them once and runs only the new position, so a step costs instead of .

Where the time goes

, model: a step at position costs ms recomputing everything, ms with the cache. The tiny model gains nothing: vs ms for tokens, because Python overhead beats the matmuls.

Mathematically

Without a cache, step runs a forward on positions: attention costs per block and the projections , so writing tokens after a prompt of costs . With a cache the new position computes its own , , (), attends over stored rows () and the MLP (): per step, linear in . The price is memory: floats per sequence.

03 · Engine · The contract

The engine's contract: a generator of tokens with reasons

Everything above folds into one small object that owns the cache and the budget, takes ids, and yields one token at a time. Yielding is what makes streaming, cancellation and batching possible.

class Engine:                               # owns: the cache, the budget, the rng
    def stream(self, ids, max_new=60, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None,
               stop_strs=(), seed=1):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); text = ''
        ids = ids[-self.T:]                     # crop to the window
        kv = KVCache(self.m)
        logits = cached_step(self.m, kv, ids)   # prefill: the whole prompt at once
        for i in range(max_new):
            t = time.perf_counter()
            nxt, _ = sample(logits, rng, temperature, top_k, top_p)   # decoding policy
            text += self.tok.decode([nxt]); ids.append(nxt)
            if any(text.endswith(s) for s in stop_strs):               # stop rule, every token
                yield nxt, time.perf_counter() - t, 'stop'; return
            if kv.t >= self.T:                                         # window full: re-prefill
                kv = KVCache(self.m); ids = ids[-self.T:]
                logits = cached_step(self.m, kv, ids)
            else:
                logits = cached_step(self.m, kv, [nxt])                # one position, cached
            yield nxt, time.perf_counter() - t, 'budget' if i == max_new - 1 else None

Streaming

The caller receives "m" ms after the prefill and the rest at ms each; time to first token = prefill + one step. A user reads while the model writes.

Batching

sequences share one forward: logits , one sample and one cache per row. Production engines add and drop rows between steps (continuous batching), so nobody waits for the longest request.

Cancellation

A generator can be dropped at any token: the loop simply stops calling next(). A function that returns the whole string cannot be interrupted.

Engine.stream from the scratch script (__init__ elided). Timeline: stream from "the cat sat on the " (cropped to ), , seed 1, stop " . ": prefill ms, six tokens "mat . " at , , , , , ms, reason stop.

Visually

  • Step 1: the code, with the five responsibilities marked in comments: crop, prefill, decode, stop, cache. Step 2: the timeline of one real call: a prefill block, then six token arrivals with their measured gaps, ending at the stop string. Steps 3–4: what the generator shape buys.

Mathematically

Latency of a response of tokens: . Prefill is one forward over prompt ids (parallel, compute-bound); each step is one cached forward over one id (sequential, memory-bound). Throughput of a batch of rows is about tokens per step while the step time barely grows, which is why servers batch.

Numerically

Prefill of ids: ms. Steps: , , , , , ms. Whole answer "mat . " in under ms. For comparison, the shipped generate under autograd takes ms per token on this model, ms under no_grad(): the graph it builds and discards is a tenth of its time even at this size.

In your code

Turning GPT.generate into this is mostly deletion and one yield: crop, check a stop condition, yield instead of concatenate, and wrap the forward in no_grad(). The cache can come later; the contract (tokens, timing, reason) is what the rest of the harness depends on.

Check yourself

  • Why is the time to first token dominated by the prompt and not by the model's depth? Prefill processes all prompt positions before the first sample; for long prompts that one forward is the largest single cost.

04 · Context · The window

The window is the model's only memory: exactly slots

Whatever the model should know for this answer must be among the ids of this forward: instructions, history, tool results, and room for the answer. Context management is the bookkeeping of those slots.

Budget

The answer also needs slots. The harness keeps a reserve for the output ( of here) and must fit everything else into the rest. Nothing outside the window exists for the model.

A system prompt alone does not fit

"You are a helpful assistant." is characters, of them <UNK> (Y, p, f, i are not in the corpus): ids for a -slot window. The tokenizer is part of the budget: unknown characters cost a slot and carry nothing.

Four messages need slots

A short chat (system, user, assistant, user) with role markers takes ids: , plus the opening marker for the answer. Four times the window.

The same rule at every scale

GPT-2: . A modern model: or more. The arithmetic is the same: every instruction, document and tool result is paid for in slots, and the answer's reserve comes first.

Counts from CharTokenizer (vocab of the -character corpus, ) and a scratch encode_chat that adds four special ids (–) for <|sys|>, <|user|>, <|asst|>, <|end|>. Chat: sys "reply in corpus words", user "the cat sat on the", asst " mat .", user "and the dog ?".

Visually

  • Step 1: the window as slots; the last are hatched as the reserve for the answer. Step 2: the system prompt laid over it: chips, the grey ones are <UNK>, overflowing the bar. Step 3: the four-message chat as a -chip strip, coloured by role, with the window drawn under it for scale. Step 4: the same bar for GPT-2 and a window, log scale.

Mathematically

Constraint per forward: , where is the reserve for the output and every is a token count under the model's tokenizer. The attention cost of the forward is per block, so the budget is also a latency budget: filling the window costs time as well as slots.

Numerically

, , budget . System prompt: ids ( id ). Chat: ids, of which are role markers. BPE trained on the corpus with writes the -character corpus in tokens ( characters per token): a tokenizer is the first compression of the window.

In your code

PositionalEncoding.forward raises when seq_len > max_seq_len; that is the hard edge of the window. CharTokenizer.encode maps every unknown character to unk_id . Special tokens do not exist yet: build_vocab would need to append them after the characters so that ids stay stable.

Check yourself

  • Why reserve slots for the answer instead of filling the window with context? Each generated token takes a slot; with no reserve the first generated token already overflows (or forces a crop that drops the beginning of the prompt).

04 · Context · The chat template

Chat template: roles become tokens the model must learn

A conversation is a list of (role, text) pairs; the model sees one flat id sequence. The template is the agreed rendering: a marker id before each message, an end id after it, and an opening marker for the answer.

Four new ids:

<|sys|> , <|user|> , <|asst|> , <|end|> . Each needs a row in the token table and in the head ( and new weights), and both start random.

Render: messages → ids

For each message: marker, characters, . Then to open the answer. The chat becomes ids: the model is asked to continue after <|asst|>.

Parse: ids → message

The engine stops at id , so <|end|> is the stop token. Everything the model wrote between and is the assistant message. The next user turn is appended and rendered again.

Protocol, not magic

The tiny model never saw ids – and would treat them as noise. Chat models are fine-tuned on rendered chats until they emit after an answer: the template is a contract between data and code.

encode_chat in the scratch script: ids – appended to the CharTokenizer vocabulary; the -id strip is its real output for the four-message chat; per-message lengths , , , , plus one opening marker.

Visually

  • Step 1: the vocabulary table extended by four rows. Step 2: the four messages on the left, their rendered ids as a strip on the right, markers in the role colours, characters in grey, and the id numbers under the first few. Step 3: the model's answer region between and , and where the harness cuts. Step 4: the training-side of the contract.

Mathematically

. The map is injective, so parse is its left inverse: the harness can always recover the messages from the ids. Training a chat model minimises cross-entropy on the assistant spans only (the loss is masked on user and system tokens), which is how the model learns to produce and nothing after it.

Numerically

Chat ids: [18, 14, 7, 0, 10, 0, 1, 0, …, 21, 19, …, 21, 20]: ids, markers, characters ( of them <UNK>: p, y, i, w and ? are outside the corpus vocabulary). Markers are of the slots in this short chat; in a long chat they are negligible.

In your code

Nothing renders chats yet. Minimal additions: CharTokenizer gets a special list appended to vocab after the characters; EmbeddingLayer and GPT are built with the enlarged ; a render(messages) function in the harness; Engine.stream gets stop_ids=(21,). Training data must be rendered the same way.

Check yourself

  • Why is the stop token an id rather than a string here? An id is unambiguous and cannot appear inside normal text; a string stop rule could fire on user content.

04 · Context · When it does not fit

When it does not fit: drop, compress, or retrieve

Every real conversation outgrows the window. Three moves, usually combined: truncation drops the past, compaction keeps a summary of it, retrieval keeps it outside and brings back the few pieces the next turn needs.

Truncate: drop the oldest non-system message

Context.fit on the -slot window: a -id chat drops messages, keeping the system marker and the latest user turn: ids, exactly the budget. Deterministic, instant, forgetful.

Compact: replace history with its summary

Ask the model (or a smaller one) to summarise the dropped messages into a few lines, and keep those lines in the system slot. Costs one extra model call; keeps the gist, loses the exact words.

Retrieve: fetch only what matters

Store messages and documents in an index; each turn, fetch the few most similar to the new question and put only those in the window: relevant, not recent (retrieval-augmented generation).

Also: a better tokenizer

BPE on the corpus with writes the same characters in ids: more words per window before any of the three moves above.

Context.fit from the scratch harness, token-counted (one id per character, one per role marker, one per end marker, plus the opening <|asst|>): ids, messages dropped. BPETokenizer(vocab_size=40).train([text]) then encode(text): tokens.

Visually

  • Step 1: the -id chat over the -id budget; the two oldest non-system messages are struck out and the strip shrinks to . Step 2: the same chat with the struck-out messages replaced by a short summary chip. Step 3: the history moved into a store on the left, and two retrieved pieces brought back into the window. Step 4: the corpus under the character tokenizer ( chips) and under BPE ( chips).

Mathematically

Truncation keeps the suffix of the history that fits: . Compaction replaces by with . Retrieval chooses a subset maximising under , with usually a dot product of embeddings, the same operation as attention scores, done outside the model.

Numerically

Chat before fit: sys "" ( ids), user "the cat sat" (), asst "on the mat ." (), user "the dog" (), opening marker (): . Budget . After dropping the first user and the assistant turn: . BPE: characters → tokens at , first tokens "th", ""… (the scratch BPE's </w> handling leaves gaps: a bug to note, not fix, in BPETokenizer.encode).

In your code

Context.fit is a while loop over self.msgs with a count function; the only policy decision is which message to drop (never the system one). BPETokenizer.train and encode exist in src/core/tokenization.py; their per-word end marker makes some words decode to <UNK>, which the window slide's numbers show.

Check yourself

  • Which of the three moves changes what the model is conditioned on without changing any id it has seen before? Truncation: it only removes a prefix. Compaction and retrieval both insert new ids.

05 · The loop · State machine

The agent loop: a state machine around generate

Render the context, let the engine write until it stops, parse the text. Either it is an answer and the loop ends, or it is a request to run something, and the result goes back into the context for another pass.

Five states, two exits

render → generate → parse → execute → append → render … The exits are final (the model answered) and budget (max_steps reached). The model never sees the states; it sees ids and writes ids.

A real run: four passes

User: "what is 2+3, and what is a mat?" Pass 0: tool call calc → . Pass 1: tool call shell → denied. Pass 2: lookup → "where the cat sat". Pass 3: final answer. Nine messages in the context at the end, characters.

Why a loop and not a longer prompt

Tool results are facts the model cannot produce. The only way to condition the next tokens on a fact is to put it in the window and run again: the loop exists because the model is a pure function of its window.

agent_loop(model_fn, ctx, max_steps=6) from the scratch harness, with a scripted stand-in for the model (the tiny GPT cannot emit tool syntax); the four trace events shown are its real output. Everything except model_fn is the production shape.

Visually

  • Step 1: the state machine. Boxes are harness code; the amber box is the engine call; the diamond is the parser's decision; dashed edges are exits. Step 2: the four passes of the real run drawn as a trace along the machine (pass number, what the model wrote, what came back). Step 3: the reason the loop exists.

Mathematically

A transition system with . The model is the only non-deterministic transition: generate samples . if has no tool call, else execute. Termination is guaranteed by the step budget: at most max_steps model calls, at most max_steps max_new tokens.

Numerically

Passes: ( tool, final). Model calls: . Tool executions: (one call denied before execution). Final context: messages (sys, user, then asst/tool pairs, then asst). Each model call here takes microseconds because the stand-in is a lookup; with the tiny GPT engine a pass costs the prefill of the rendered context plus one token per step.

In your code

The loop is lines of plain Python: for step in range(max_steps): prompt = ctx.render(); out = model_fn(prompt); m = CALL.search(out); …. model_fn is the seam: in production it is Engine.stream joined into a string; here it is the stub. Swapping one for the other changes no other line.

Check yourself

  • What happens if the model writes a tool call and an answer in the same output? The parser decides; the usual rule is "a tool call wins, the answer text is discarded or kept as a thought", and that rule is harness code, not model behaviour.

05 · The loop · Tools

Tools: the model writes a call, the harness executes it

A tool is a function with a name and an argument format. The model is told both, writes a call as text, and the harness finds it, checks it, runs it and writes the result back as a message. The model never executes anything.

Schema: what the model is told

A registry maps names to functions: calc(expr), lookup(word). Their descriptions are rendered into the system message, so the model can only call what it has read about.

Grammar: what the model writes

<tool>calc:2+3</tool>. A regular expression finds it. Production harnesses use JSON with a schema check; the idea is the same: a parseable span inside free text.

Result: a message, never an exception

The return value, or the error text, is appended as <result>5</result> in a tool message. The model reads it on the next pass. A crash in a tool becomes error: ZeroDivisionError in the context, and the loop continues.

Tools are how facts enter the window

Calculators, search, files, databases, other models: each is a function. The model's job is to choose and to phrase; correctness of the result is the tool's.

TOOLS, CALL and the execute branch of agent_loop in the scratch harness; the sequence shown is trace events 0 and 2 of the real run: calc("2+3") → "5", lookup("mat") → "where the cat sat".

Visually

  • A sequence diagram with four lanes: context, model, parser and policy, tool. Step 1: the registry rendered into the context. Step 2: the model's text with the call span framed, the parser extracting name and argument. Step 3: the tool runs, the result message is appended, and the next pass starts. Step 4: the principle.

Mathematically

A tool call is a pair recognised by a grammar inside the model's output : . The harness computes and appends it, so the next distribution is . Nothing about leaks into ; the model only learns, from training examples, when writing a call is likely to lead to a good continuation.

Numerically

Registry: tools. Calls in the run: written, executed, denied. Results: "5" ( character) and "where the cat sat" (). Each result costs its characters plus for the <result> markers in the window: characters of context after the run, which would be windows of the tiny model.

In your code

TOOLS = {'calc': …, 'lookup': …}; CALL = re.compile(r'<tool>(\w+):(.*?)</tool>'); execution is TOOLS[name](arg) inside try/except, and both branches end in ctx.add('tool', f'<result>{res}</result>'). A JSON protocol replaces the regex with json.loads plus a schema check.

Check yourself

  • Why must a tool error be returned as text instead of raised? Raising ends the loop with no answer; returning lets the model read the error and try another call or explain.

05 · The loop · The policy gate

The policy gate: between parse and execute, in code

Once the parser has a (name, argument) pair, a rule decides: allow, deny, or ask a person. In the run, the stand-in model asked for shell: rm -rf /; the gate wrote "denied" back as a message and the loop went on.

Three verdicts

allow: run it. deny: do not run; tell the model why. ask: pause the loop and let a person decide. Unknown tool names fall to ask by default, never to allow.

Sandbox: the fourth verdict is "allow, but in here"

Even an allowed tool runs with limits: a working directory, a time limit, no network, a read-only file system. The gate decides whether; the sandbox decides how far.

Retries and budgets

A denied or failed call is a message, so the model may try again. The loop counts: max_steps bounds passes, and a per-tool counter can stop a model that repeats a failing call.

Why it lives here

Before the parser there is only text; after execution it is too late. The gate is the one place where the intended action is explicit and nothing has happened yet.

POLICY = {'calc': 'allow', 'lookup': 'allow', 'shell': 'deny'} with POLICY.get(name, 'ask'); trace event 1 of the real run: model wrote <tool>shell:rm -rf /</tool>, verdict deny, result "error: tool shell is deny", loop continued to event 2.

Visually

  • Step 1: the pass-1 event: the call, the gate's table lookup, the deny verdict written back as a result message. Step 2: the sandbox drawn as a box around the tool lane. Step 3: the counters on the loop. Step 4: the gate's position between parse and execute, marked on the state machine.

Mathematically

; the loop executes only if . Because gate reads only and not the model's prose, no text the model generates can change the verdict except by changing the pair, which is exactly what the gate inspects. Safety properties are therefore properties of a small, total, testable function.

Numerically

Policy table: entries. Verdicts in the run: allow, deny, allow. Executions: . The deny cost one pass and one result message ("error: tool shell is deny") and had no side effect.

In your code

In the scratch loop: verdict = POLICY.get(name, 'ask'); if verdict != 'allow' or name not in TOOLS: res = f'error: tool {name} is {verdict}'. An "ask" verdict in a real harness suspends the loop, stores the pending call, and resumes with the person's answer as the result.

Check yourself

  • Could the gate be implemented as a system-prompt instruction instead? No: an instruction changes , which is probabilistic; the gate must be a deterministic check outside the model.

05 · The loop · The code

The whole loop in thirty lines of plain Python

class Context:                                       # owns: the messages, the budget
    def __init__(self, T, reserve): self.T, self.reserve, self.msgs = T, reserve, []
    def add(self, role, text): self.msgs.append((role, text))
    def render(self): return ''.join(f'<|{r}|>{t}<|end|>' for r, t in self.msgs) + '<|asst|>'
    def fit(self, count):                            # drop the oldest non-system message until it fits
        while count(self.render()) > self.T - self.reserve and len(self.msgs) > 1:
            self.msgs.pop(1 if self.msgs[0][0] == 'sys' else 0)

TOOLS  = {'calc': lambda s: str(eval(s, {'__builtins__': {}})), 'lookup': lambda w: FACTS.get(w, 'unknown')}
CALL   = re.compile(r'<tool>(\w+):(.*?)</tool>', re.S)
POLICY = {'calc': 'allow', 'lookup': 'allow', 'shell': 'deny'}

def agent_loop(model_fn, ctx, max_steps=6):          # owns: the step count, the trace
    trace = []
    for step in range(max_steps):
        out = model_fn(ctx.render())                 # render → generate (Engine.stream, joined)
        m = CALL.search(out)                         # parse
        if not m:
            ctx.add('asst', out); trace.append((step, 'final', out)); return out, trace
        name, arg = m.group(1), m.group(2).strip(); ctx.add('asst', out)
        verdict = POLICY.get(name, 'ask')            # policy gate
        if verdict != 'allow' or name not in TOOLS: res = f'error: tool {name} is {verdict}'
        else:
            try: res = TOOLS[name](arg)              # execute
            except Exception as e: res = f'error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}'
        ctx.add('tool', f'<result>{res}</result>')   # append, then loop
        trace.append((step, 'tool', name, arg, verdict, res))
    trace.append((max_steps, 'budget')); return None, trace

Where the state is

ctx.msgs (the conversation), step (the budget), trace (the record), and inside the engine the KV cache and the rng. The model object has none.

The trace of the run

0 tool calc "2+3" allow → 5
1 tool shell "rm -rf /" deny → error
2 tool lookup "mat" allow → where the cat sat
3 final "the answer is 5 and the mat is where the cat sat ."

What is missing on purpose

Streaming the final answer to the user, the "ask" verdict pausing the loop, structured (JSON) calls, parallel tool calls, and a per-tool budget. Each is a few lines in the same places.

The scratch harness, verbatim except for FACTS (a two-entry dict) and the trace tuples (dicts in the script). Run: Context(T=400, reserve=40), sys "use tools when needed", user "what is 2+3, and what is a mat?", stand-in model; output as shown.

Visually

  • The listing is annotated with the state-machine names from slide 14 in the comments: render, generate, parse, gate, execute, append. Step 1: the state. Step 2: the trace. Step 3: what a production loop adds.

Mathematically

Total work of a task: . Because the context grows by every output and result, pass 's prefill costs grow with ; with a KV cache shared across passes (prefix caching) the already-seen prefix is not recomputed, which is why production harnesses keep the context append-only.

Numerically

lines for the loop, for the engine, for the cache, for sampling: about lines of harness around the model modules. Nine messages and characters of context at the end of the run.

In your code

None of it is in src/. If it moves there, the natural home is a new src/core/harness.py with Engine, Context, agent_loop, and a KVCache that MultiHeadAttention.forward accepts as an optional argument.

Check yourself

  • Which line would you change to run the tiny GPT instead of the stand-in? None in the loop: pass model_fn = lambda p: ''.join(tok.decode([t]) for t, _, _ in eng.stream(tok.encode(p))).

06 · Around the loop · Observability

Observability: every token and every pass is an event

The harness is the only place that sees everything: the rendered context, the sampled ids, the time per step, the calls, verdicts and results. Recorded with the seed, they make any run reproducible.

Token events: the engine's stream

Each yield is an event: id, text, milliseconds, reason. From them: time to first token (prefill + one step), tokens per second, and why the answer ended.

Pass events: the loop's trace

Each pass: what the model wrote, the parsed call, the verdict, the result, the time. From them: passes per task, tool error rate, denied calls, context growth.

Replay

Model weights + seed + the trace = the run. Sampling used default_rng(1); the same seed gives the same characters on slide 8 whether or not a stop rule is set.

What to alert on

Reason budget rising (answers cut off), passes per task rising (the model is flailing), tool errors, time per token rising (context too long, cache missing).

Left: the six token events of Engine.stream from "the cat sat on the " (stop " . "): prefill ms, steps / / / / / ms. Right: the four pass events of agent_loop. Both are the lists the scratch harness returned.

Visually

  • Step 1: a table of the token events with a bar for each step's time and the derived KPIs. Step 2: the pass events as a second table. Step 3: the replay equation and the alert list.

Mathematically

Given , the seed, and the harness settings, the run is a deterministic function of the user input and the tool results: record those, and every intermediate value can be recomputed. Metrics are reductions over events: ; ; ; .

Numerically

Stream: tokens, ms total, ms per token, tokens per second on this CPU for a -parameter model; TTFT ms. Trace: passes, tool events, error (the deny), error rate , context characters.

In your code

Trainer.history is the training-side equivalent (loss per epoch, learning rates). The scratch engine yields (token, seconds, reason) and the loop appends dicts to trace; a real harness writes the same records as structured logs with a request id.

Check yourself

  • Why record the seed and not just the output? With the seed you can rerun with one change (a new policy, a new weight) and see what differs; the output alone cannot be perturbed.

06 · Around the loop · Evaluation

Evaluation: the same loop, fixed inputs, and a scorer

Drive the model the way users do and compare with what should have happened, at three levels: the model alone, a task suite through the engine, and the whole loop. The third reuses everything above.

Level 1: the model, teacher-forced

Feed every training window, compare argmax with the true next character: of positions correct, mean loss , perplexity . No sampling, no harness: a pure function test.

Level 2: a task suite through the engine

Five prompts, three greedy characters each, exact match: . "the rat sat on the " → "mat" is a prompt not in the corpus; the model generalised from "sat on the".

Level 3: the loop

Fixed user goals, the real tools (or recorded responses), the real policy; score the final answer, count passes and denials. The agent loop with a scorer appended: no new machinery.

Use it as a gate

Run the suite on every checkpoint and every harness change; a drop blocks the change. Seeds fixed, where possible, so the only variable is what you changed.

Level 1: full_forward on the windows ( vs ; NLL from the softmax rows). Level 2: Engine.stream(prompt, max_new=3, temperature=0) for the five prompts; exact match against the corpus continuation. The scratch script's ev block.

Visually

  • Step 1: the loss curve of the training run () and the KPIs of the teacher-forced pass. Step 2: the suite as a table: prompt, expected, produced, pass. Step 3: the three levels stacked, with the loop level drawn as the state machine plus a scorer.

Mathematically

Level 1: , , . Level 2: . Level 3: a score function over (final answer, trace); the trace lets you score process as well as outcome (passes, denied calls, cost).

Numerically

Accuracy over positions, NLL , perplexity . Suite: cat/mat, dog/log, cat ate/rat, dog ate/bun, rat sat/mat: passes. Loss at init , final , steps, s.

In your code

Trainer.evaluate(dataloader) already does level 1 (forward, loss, no gradients). Level 2 needs the engine with ; level 3 needs the loop with a stubbed tool registry. All three are table-driven: a list of (input, expected) and a scorer.

Check yourself

  • Why evaluate at ? To remove sampling noise, so that a score change reflects the model or the harness, not the seed.

06 · Around the loop · Serving

Serving: many loops for many users, one shared engine

A request arrives with a session id. The server loads that session's context, runs the loop, streams tokens back, and saves the context. The engine is the scarce resource, so requests queue and are batched into it.

Sessions: the context, stored

The loop's ctx.msgs survives between requests in a store keyed by session. The model still sees only the rendered window: the store is harness state, not model state.

The scheduler: batch into the engine

Requests wait in a queue; the engine runs one step for all active rows at once, adds rows after their prefill and drops finished ones. Throughput scales with ; latency per token stays near the single-row cost.

Limits per request

Timeout, token budget, pass budget, cancellation when the client disconnects. All are the loop's budgets, set per request, enforced by the generator being dropped.

Versions

The model, the template, the tool registry and the policy are versioned together: a context rendered under one template cannot be continued under another.

Architecture slide: no new measurement. The per-step cost on the engine is the cached-step number of slide 9 (– ms for the model); batching rows multiplies the matmul widths by while the Python overhead stays constant, which is the whole argument for a scheduler.

Visually

  • Step 1: clients, the API, the session store. Step 2: the queue and the scheduler feeding the engine with a batch; rows enter after prefill and leave at their stop. Step 3: the limits on a request. Step 4: the version tags on the four coupled parts.

Mathematically

With active rows, one step costs about for small (overhead plus a linear term) and the server produces tokens per step: throughput , rising until the matmuls saturate the hardware. Queueing theory applies: arrival rate must stay below that throughput or the queue grows without bound, which is what the timeout protects against.

Numerically

For the model, a cached step at is ms; at that is about tokens per second for the whole server. Batching to at near-constant step time would give about , which is why no production server runs .

In your code

The engine's stream handles one row; batched serving needs a cache per row and a step function over a id array, which GPT.forward already accepts: the block code is batch-first. The scheduler is a loop over a queue; no model change.

Check yourself

  • Why can a finished row be removed from the batch mid-run but a new row not be inserted without a prefill? A new row has no , rows yet; its prompt must be processed before it can take part in a shared step.

Check yourself, across the deck

  • In one sentence: what is a harness? The fixed, stateful, deterministic machinery that drives a stateless core, feeds it, acts on its output, limits it and measures it.
  • Which decisions does the engine make, and which does the loop make? Engine: which token, when to stop, what to cache. Loop: what the window holds, whether to run again, whether an action is allowed.
  • Why is the KV cache a harness concern although it changes the attention code? It exists only for generation; training never needs it; the engine owns and invalidates it.
  • Why must the policy gate be code and not prompt text? Prompt text changes a probability; the gate must be a certainty.
  • How do the three harnesses (test, eval, agent) differ, in one word each? Judge: assertion, scorer, parser-and-policy.

Context: slots, reserve , a -id system prompt and a -id chat do not fit; fit() . Loop: passes, calls, executed, denied, characters of context at the end.
